patient.name: Doreen Fitzgerald
patient.setting: Acute medical ward, day 5 of admission
patient.complaint: New watery diarrhoea, abdominal cramps and fever while on antibiotics
background: Admitted with community-acquired pneumonia, on IV co-amoxiclav
Lives alone in Lewisham; no recent travel

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely causative organism?' where the food, the incubation time, travel or recent antibiotics give it away; bloody versus watery stool and systemic signs narrow it further.

points: Doreen, 76, day 5 of **IV co-amoxiclav** for pneumonia.
Overnight: **7 watery stools**, foul-smelling, no blood.
Crampy lower abdominal pain; feels shivery.
Also on **omeprazole**; no travel, no odd food.

steps.lead: Doreen has acute diarrhoea from a GI infection; the job is to work out **which organism**, because that decides the test and the drug.

steps.q: Which organism is most likely causing Doreen's diarrhoea?
steps.r: Hospital inpatient, over 65, on a broad-spectrum antibiotic and a PPI: **C. difficile** until proven otherwise.

steps.lead: Doreen ticks three **C. difficile** risk factors: age over 65, a penicillin antibiotic and a PPI. Typhoid is on the same card for contrast: think travel and relative bradycardia.

steps.lead: Not Doreen's picture, but the exam loves these two: **Campylobacter** (bloody, 2 to 3 days, GBS) and **Staph aureus** (vomiting within hours).

visual.title: Incubation time points to the organism
visual.label: Vomiting 3 h after a buffet
visual.caption: Hours means preformed toxin (**Staph aureus**); 2 to 3 days with blood means **Campylobacter**.

steps.lead: Doreen has not travelled, so **Giardia** is unlikely; she has not eaten undercooked chicken, so **Salmonella** is too.

points: Bowel sounds reduced; stools still frequent.
Team worries about a colonic complication.

steps.lead: Doreen's distension and tachycardia raise the fear of **toxic megacolon**; flexible sigmoidoscopy in C. difficile may show **pseudomembranes**.

steps.text: Relative bradycardia, rose spots and constipation then diarrhoea after travel is **typhoid**, not C. difficile. A fast pulse with fever is the expected response; a slow one is the clue.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial / diagnostic investigation?': stool sample for most diarrhoea, but **blood culture** for typhoid. Watch for 'no investigation needed' in mild self-limiting cases.

steps.q: Doreen is over 65, febrile and in hospital. Does she need tests?
o: No, it is a clinical diagnosis
Yes, bloods and a stool sample
steps.r: Most diarrhoea needs no tests, but she is **severe, hospital-acquired and frail**: send bloods and a stool sample.

steps.lead: Clinical assessment comes first; Doreen's fever and frequent stools make her **severe**, so U&Es and FBC are justified.

steps.title: Doreen's bloods, day 5
steps.text: High white count and a rising creatinine from dehydration; low potassium from stool losses.

visual.title: White cell count in C. difficile
visual.label: Doreen 18.4
visual.caption: A white count above **15** (UK standard practice) marks severe C. difficile infection.

steps.lead: Doreen's stool goes for **microscopy, culture and PCR**, which includes testing for C. difficile toxin.
**Stool culture** is the gold standard for bacterial diarrhoea; if Doreen had returned from South Asia with a stepwise fever, you would send **blood cultures** for typhoid.

steps.text: Typhoid is a bloodstream infection: the diagnostic test is **blood culture**, not stool culture. Stool culture is the default for the rest.
Campylobacter grows at **42°C** and is a Gram-negative curved rod: a lab clue the papers use.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': oral rehydration for most, **oral vancomycin** for C. difficile, **fidaxomicin** for relapse, **metronidazole** for Giardia. Antibiotics are the exception, not the rule.

steps.q: Stool PCR confirms C. difficile toxin. Which drug first?
steps.r: **Oral vancomycin** is first-line for C. difficile; stop the culprit antibiotic if possible. Loperamide risks toxic megacolon.

steps.lead: Doreen gets **oral vancomycin** plus fluids and potassium; because she is septic, **IV metronidazole** is added.

steps.title: C. difficile pathway
nodes: Isolate in a side room, soap-and-water hand washing
Stop or review the culprit antibiotic and PPI
Oral vancomycin (add IV metronidazole if septic)
steps.caption: Review the drugs that caused it as well as treating the infection.

visual.title: Response to oral vancomycin
visual.caption: Stool frequency and white count fall together as treatment works.

points: Stool again positive for C. difficile toxin.
GP calls the hospital team for advice.

steps.lead: Doreen has relapsed **within 12 weeks**, so she needs **oral fidaxomicin**. Metronidazole for Giardia is on the same card.
On the ward Doreen stayed in a side room; staff used gloves, aprons and soap and water.

steps.text: Alcohol gel does not kill **C. difficile spores**: wash hands with soap and water. Avoid antimotility drugs such as loperamide in C. difficile or bloody diarrhoea.

steps.lead: Doreen's care follows national gastroenteritis guidance; C. difficile and food poisoning outbreaks are reported to public health.

steps.text: For most adults with infectious diarrhoea the answer is **ORS**, then **IV 0.9% saline** if severely dry. Antibiotics only for specific organisms or severe bacterial infection.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: why typhoid is systemic, why Campylobacter causes Guillain-Barré, why Staph aureus acts in hours, how C. difficile toxins make pseudomembranes.

steps.lead: Doreen's antibiotics wiped out her normal colonic flora, letting C. difficile overgrow and release **toxins A and B**.

steps.title: From antibiotics to pseudomembranes
nodes: C. difficile spores germinate and overgrow
steps.caption: Spores survive alcohol and spread on hands and surfaces.

steps.lead: Contrast Doreen's colonic illness with typhoid: S. typhi gets in through **M cells in Peyer's patches** and spreads in the blood.

steps.q: A man develops leg weakness 2 weeks after bloody diarrhoea. What links the two?
steps.r: Antibodies to **Campylobacter** lipooligosaccharide cross-react with nerve **gangliosides**: Guillain-Barré syndrome.

steps.lead: Campylobacter's link with **Guillain-Barré** is a favourite applied science question.
Staph aureus acts in **1 to 6 hours** because the toxin is already made in the food; nothing has to grow in the gut.

steps.text: Short incubation = **preformed toxin** (Staph aureus, also Bacillus cereus). Longer incubation = organisms must multiply first (Salmonella, Campylobacter).

mcq.q: Which sign accompanies the fever in typhoid?
mcq.r: **Faget sign**: pulse slower than expected for the fever.

mcq.q: Which neurological complication follows Campylobacter jejuni?
Vomiting 2 hours after a picnic suggests which organism?
Which food is classically linked to Salmonella?
What are pseudomembranes in C. difficile colitis?
mcq.r: Thumb-printing is toxic megacolon on imaging.
S. typhi is systemic; **blood culture** is the test.

mcq.q: What is the gold standard test for infectious diarrhoea?
mcq.r: Stool culture; most mild cases need no test.

mcq.q: First-line treatment for a first episode of C. difficile?
mcq.r: Fidaxomicin is for relapse within 12 weeks; IV vancomycin does not reach the colon.

mcq.q: Why does Staph aureus food poisoning start within hours?
mcq.r: The toxin is already in the food.

points.p: Most cases: clinical diagnosis, no investigation
points.why: Unless severe, bloody, persistent or immunocompromised.
Low potassium and AKI are common.

points.p: Stool microscopy, culture and PCR; culture is the gold standard

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fluids first; antibiotics are the exception.

points.why: Or unable to keep fluids down.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: vancomycin, then fidaxomicin; metronidazole IV only if septic.

prompts.q: Explain the mechanisms: typhoid's systemic illness, Campylobacter's GBS, Staph aureus's speed, C. difficile damage.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: each organism has one mechanism to learn.

points.p: Typhoid: invades M cells in Peyer's patches, spreads via reticuloendothelial system
Campylobacter: molecular mimicry, lipooligosaccharide antibodies hit nerve gangliosides
C. difficile: toxins A and B disrupt epithelial cytoskeleton, causing pseudomembranes

glossary.C. difficile: Clostridioides difficile, a spore-forming bacterium causing antibiotic-associated colitis.
glossary.Clostridioides difficile: Spore-forming gut bacterium that overgrows after antibiotics and releases toxins A and B.
glossary.Campylobacter: Gram-negative curved rod from undercooked meat or unpasteurised milk; commonest bacterial cause of bloody diarrhoea in the UK.
glossary.Salmonella: Gram-negative bacterium from undercooked poultry and eggs; typhi causes typhoid fever.
glossary.Salmonella typhi: The Salmonella serotype causing typhoid fever, a systemic illness spread faeco-orally.
glossary.typhoid: Systemic infection with Salmonella typhi: stepwise fever, relative bradycardia, rose spots, splenomegaly.
glossary.Giardia: Protozoan parasite from contaminated water causing watery diarrhoea, bloating and malabsorption.
glossary.Staph aureus: Staphylococcus aureus; its preformed toxin in food causes vomiting within 1 to 6 hours.
glossary.relative bradycardia: A pulse slower than expected for the height of the fever.
glossary.Faget sign: Relative bradycardia with fever; classic in typhoid.
glossary.rose spots: Faint pink macules on the trunk in typhoid fever.
glossary.pseudomembranous colitis: Colitis with raised yellow plaques of fibrin and debris, caused by C. difficile toxins.
glossary.pseudomembranes: Raised yellow plaques of fibrin, mucus and dead cells on the colonic mucosa.
glossary.toxic megacolon: Acute, life-threatening dilation of the colon with systemic toxicity.
glossary.thumb-printing: Thickened, oedematous colonic wall folds seen on imaging in severe colitis.
glossary.Guillain-Barré syndrome: Immune-mediated ascending paralysis with lost reflexes, often after Campylobacter.
glossary.GBS: Guillain-Barré syndrome: post-infectious ascending areflexic weakness.
glossary.molecular mimicry: Antibodies against a microbe cross-react with similar-looking host molecules.
glossary.gangliosides: Glycolipids on nerve cell membranes and myelin, targeted in Guillain-Barré syndrome.
glossary.lipooligosaccharide: Sugar-lipid molecule on the Campylobacter surface that resembles nerve gangliosides.
glossary.enterotoxin: A toxin that acts on the intestine to cause secretion, vomiting or diarrhoea.
glossary.preformed toxin: Toxin made in the food before eating, so symptoms start within hours.
glossary.incubation period: Time between exposure and the first symptoms.
glossary.M cells: Specialised epithelial cells over Peyer's patches that sample gut contents; S. typhi enters through them.
glossary.Peyer's patches: Lymphoid tissue clusters in the ileal wall.
glossary.reticuloendothelial system: Phagocytic cells in liver, spleen, bone marrow and lymph nodes.
glossary.ORS: Oral rehydration solution: glucose and salts that drive water absorption in the gut.
glossary.PPI: Proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole; raises C. difficile risk.
glossary.PPIs: Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole; they raise C. difficile risk.
glossary.vancomycin: Glycopeptide antibiotic; given orally for C. difficile because it stays in the gut.
glossary.fidaxomicin: Narrow-spectrum oral antibiotic for C. difficile relapse.
glossary.metronidazole: Antibiotic for anaerobes and protozoa; treats Giardia and is added IV in septic C. difficile.
glossary.clindamycin: Antibiotic classically linked to C. difficile infection.
glossary.loperamide: Antimotility drug; avoided in C. difficile and bloody diarrhoea.
glossary.PCR: Polymerase chain reaction: detects pathogen DNA or RNA in a sample.
glossary.proctoscopy: Looking at the anal canal and rectum with a short rigid scope.
glossary.sigmoidoscopy: Camera examination of the rectum and sigmoid colon.
glossary.steatorrhoea: Pale, greasy, foul-smelling stools from undigested fat.
glossary.malabsorption: Impaired absorption of nutrients from the gut.
glossary.faeco-oral: Spread when traces of faeces reach the mouth via hands, food or water.
glossary.notifiable: Must be reported to public health by law, such as food poisoning and typhoid.
glossary.U&Es: Urea and electrolytes: blood tests of kidney function, sodium and potassium.

technique.stem: A 38 year old man has profuse bloody diarrhoea with crampy abdominal pain and fever. Three days ago he ate chicken at a barbecue. He had aching muscles and a headache the day before the diarrhoea started.
technique.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?

steps.x: It asks for an organism: use the food, the timing and the stool type.
Bloody stool, onset at about 3 days, undercooked meat and a **flu-like prodrome** all fit one organism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bloody diarrhoea 2 to 3 days after poorly cooked chicken with a prodrome: **Campylobacter**.

elim: No antibiotics or hospital stay.
Watery, bloating, travel; not bloody.
Poultry too, but onset is 12–48 h with nausea and vomiting; the prodrome and blood favour Campylobacter.
Vomiting within 1–6 hours, non-bloody.

steps.x: **A. Campylobacter jejuni.** Rule: bloody + 2 to 3 days + undercooked meat + prodrome = Campylobacter.

technique.stem: A 29 year old woman has had a fever for 10 days that rises a little each day. She returned from Bangladesh 2 weeks ago. She has abdominal pain and constipation. Her temperature is 39.4°C and pulse rate 76 bpm. There are faint pink macules on her trunk and her spleen is palpable.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Stool microscopy for ova, cysts and parasites

steps.x: It asks for the diagnostic test, so first name the disease.

clues: temperature is 39.4°C and pulse rate 76 bpm
steps.x: Stepwise fever, South Asia, **relative bradycardia**, rose spots and splenomegaly.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: This is **typhoid**, a systemic infection, so the diagnostic test is **blood culture**.

elim: May show splenomegaly but cannot name the organism.
The gold standard for most diarrhoea, but typhoid is diagnosed on blood culture.
For Giardia and parasites, not S. typhi.
Malaria must be excluded in a febrile traveller, but this picture is typhoid.

steps.x: **B. Blood culture.** Rule: typhoid lives in the blood, so **blood culture**.

technique.stem: A 81 year old woman in a care home has 6 watery stools a day. She finished a course of clindamycin 1 week ago. Stool testing is positive for C. difficile toxin. She is drinking well. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management of a confirmed first episode of C. difficile.
Confirmed C. difficile after clindamycin; not septic; first episode.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First-line for C. difficile: **oral vancomycin** with fluids and isolation.

elim: Antimotility drugs risk toxic megacolon.
Second-line, for relapse within 12 weeks.
Used for Giardia; the notes give oral vancomycin first-line for C. difficile.
Supportive care alone is for Staph aureus or viral illness, not proven C. difficile.

steps.x: **E. Oral vancomycin.** Rule: C. difficile first episode = oral vancomycin; relapse = fidaxomicin.

technique.stem: A 34 year old man has diarrhoea, abdominal pain and vomiting. Two weeks ago he had bloody diarrhoea after eating undercooked chicken. He now has tingling in his feet and weakness in both legs that is spreading upwards. Knee and ankle reflexes are absent.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his weakness?
o: Direct bacterial invasion of peripheral nerves

steps.x: A mechanism question: name the illness first, then explain it.

clues: weakness in both legs that is spreading upwards
steps.x: Campylobacter, then ascending areflexic weakness 2 weeks later: **Guillain-Barré syndrome**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: GBS after Campylobacter is **molecular mimicry**: antibodies to lipooligosaccharide hit myelin gangliosides.

elim: Campylobacter does not invade nerves; the damage is immune.
Causes weakness but not areflexic ascending weakness 2 weeks later.
That is botulism (descending) or Staph aureus (GI only).
Would give brisk reflexes and a sensory level.

steps.x: **A. Antibodies cross-reacting with nerve gangliosides.** Rule: Campylobacter then GBS = molecular mimicry.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man has had profuse vomiting and watery diarrhoea for 3 hours. He ate chicken sandwiches and cream cakes at a wedding buffet 2 hours before symptoms began; the food had been left out in the sun. Several other guests are unwell. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Vomiting within 1–6 hours of unrefrigerated food is Staph aureus preformed enterotoxin. Salmonella takes 12–48 hours.

steps.x: Organism question: the time from food to symptoms decides it.
Vomiting-dominant illness within hours of unrefrigerated food, many people affected.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Onset in **1–6 hours** means a preformed toxin: **Staph aureus**.

elim: 48–72 hours and bloody.
Linked to antibiotics, not a buffet.
Days to weeks, after travel.
12–48 hours; too soon here.

steps.x: **E. Staphylococcus aureus.** Rule: hours = Staph aureus toxin.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man has had 8 watery stools a day for 3 days. He is in hospital on day 6 of IV ceftriaxone for a urinary tract infection and takes lansoprazole. He has lower abdominal cramps. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 106 bpm and BP 112/68 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Cephalosporin, PPI and age over 65 are the C. difficile triad of risk factors. Norovirus causes outbreaks but is not antibiotic related.

steps.x: Organism question: the setting and the drug chart matter most.

clues: in hospital on day 6 of IV ceftriaxone
steps.x: Over 65, inpatient, cephalosporin and PPI: classic risk factors.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **C. difficile**.

elim: Community, undercooked meat, bloody.
Outbreaks with vomiting, lasts 1–3 days, no antibiotic link.
Undercooked poultry.
Bloody dysentery from faeco-oral spread, not antibiotic linked.

steps.x: **B. Clostridioides difficile.** Rule: antibiotics + PPI + over 65 = C. difficile.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman has had a fever for 9 days, rising in steps. She returned from visiting family in Lahore 12 days ago. She has a dull headache, abdominal pain and had constipation that has now turned to diarrhoea. Her temperature is 39.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 110/70 mmHg. Her spleen is palpable.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Stepwise fever, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), splenomegaly and constipation then diarrhoea after South Asia is typhoid.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a returning traveller with fever.

clues: constipation that has now turned to diarrhoea
steps.x: Stepwise fever, South Asia, constipation then diarrhoea, **relative bradycardia**, splenomegaly.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Typhoid fever** (Salmonella typhi).

elim: Bloody diarrhoea, liver abscess; no stepwise fever.
Bloody diarrhoea within days of meat; not a 9-day stepwise fever.
Bloating and watery stools, no high fever.
Must be excluded, but cyclical fever with tachycardia; relative bradycardia points to typhoid.

steps.x: **E. Typhoid fever.** Rule: fever with a slow pulse after South Asia = typhoid.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman has had watery diarrhoea, bloating and flatulence for 3 weeks since trekking in Nepal, where she drank stream water. Her stools are pale and greasy. She has lost 3 kg. Stool cultures at her GP were negative. Her temperature is 36.9°C.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Giardia gives watery diarrhoea, bloating and malabsorption after untreated water, with negative early stool cultures. Amoebiasis is bloody.

steps.x: Organism: chronic watery diarrhoea after travel.

clues: Stool cultures at her GP were negative
steps.x: Persistent watery, greasy stools with bloating after untreated water; negative culture.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Giardia**: causes malabsorption and is missed on routine culture.

elim: Acute and bloody.
Bloody dysentery.
High stepwise fever, systemic illness.
Hours, vomiting, self-limiting.

steps.x: **C. Giardia lamblia.** Rule: travel + bloating + greasy stools + negative culture = Giardia.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has had bloody diarrhoea and abdominal cramps for 2 days. He had a flu-like illness the day before. Three days ago he ate a rare burger and drank unpasteurised milk at a farm. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Campylobacter: undercooked meat or unpasteurised milk, 48–72 hour incubation, flu-like prodrome and bloody diarrhoea.

steps.x: Organism question with food and timing.
Bloody, 3 days after undercooked meat and unpasteurised milk, prodrome.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Campylobacter jejuni**.

elim: Reheated rice; hours.
No antibiotics.
Watery, travel, weeks.
Vomiting within hours, non-bloody.

steps.x: **B. Campylobacter jejuni.** Rule: bloody + prodrome + 2 to 4 days = Campylobacter.

practice.stem: A 79 year old woman has had worsening watery diarrhoea for 5 days after a course of co-amoxiclav. Stool is positive for C. difficile toxin. Flexible sigmoidoscopy is performed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on sigmoidoscopy?
practice.e: C. difficile toxins create pseudomembranes: raised yellow plaques 2–10mm. Cobblestoning is Crohn's.

steps.x: Finding on sigmoidoscopy in confirmed C. difficile.
C. difficile colitis complicated by pseudomembrane formation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pseudomembranous colitis**: raised yellow plaques 2–10mm.

elim: Crohn's disease.
Ulcerative colitis.
Melanosis coli from laxatives.
Seen in many infections, but proven toxin-positive colitis classically shows pseudomembranes.

steps.x: **E. Raised yellow plaques.** Rule: C. difficile on scope = yellow plaques (pseudomembranes).

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has had bloody diarrhoea 8 times a day for 4 days with abdominal pain. He ate undercooked chicken at a barbecue. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the cause?
practice.e: Bloody, severe diarrhoea needs a stool sample for microscopy, culture and PCR. Blood culture is for typhoid.

steps.x: Investigation to identify the organism.
Severe, bloody diarrhoea: this is when testing is indicated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Send stool for **microscopy, culture and PCR**; stool culture is the gold standard.

elim: Only if toxic megacolon is suspected.
For typhoid; this is enteric food poisoning.
Invasive, not first for acute infection.
Separates IBD from IBS, not organisms.

steps.x: **E. Stool microscopy, culture and PCR.** Rule: severe or bloody diarrhoea = send stool.

practice.stem: A 23 year old woman has had diarrhoea and vomiting for 24 hours after eating takeaway food. She is managing to drink. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft with mild generalised tenderness. She is otherwise well and not immunocompromised.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
practice.e: Mild, short-lived diarrhoea in a well person needs no tests. Stool culture is reserved for severe, bloody, persistent or immunocompromised cases.

steps.x: 'Next step' in mild acute diarrhoea: is any test needed?
Short history, drinking, normal observations, no blood, not immunocompromised.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Most cases are a **clinical diagnosis**; no test needed unless severe, bloody, persistent or immunocompromised.

elim: No surgical sign.
Not febrile or septic.
Gold standard, but only when severe, bloody, persistent or immunocompromised.
For severe dehydration, which she does not have.

steps.x: **C. Clinical diagnosis with no investigations.** Rule: mild and well = clinical diagnosis.

practice.stem: A 69 year old man has diarrhoea 6 times a day. He finished a 10 day course of oral vancomycin for C. difficile infection 5 weeks ago and had recovered. Stool is again positive for C. difficile toxin. His temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: C. difficile relapse within 12 weeks of the first episode is treated with oral fidaxomicin. FMT is for repeated recurrences.

steps.x: Management of a recurrence.

clues: again positive for C. difficile toxin
steps.x: Relapse **within 12 weeks** of the first episode.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Second-line: **oral fidaxomicin**.

elim: Reserved for multiple recurrences.
An add-on if septic; he is not.
Risks toxic megacolon.
Used for a first episode; the relapse drug is fidaxomicin.

steps.x: **D. Oral fidaxomicin.** Rule: relapse within 12 weeks = fidaxomicin.

practice.stem: A 33 year old man has had watery diarrhoea and bloating for 4 weeks after a trip to India. Stool microscopy shows Giardia lamblia cysts. He is otherwise well.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Giardiasis is treated with metronidazole. Vancomycin is for C. difficile.

steps.x: Treatment of a named organism.
Proven persistent giardiasis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Metronidazole**.

elim: Used for some bacterial infections, not Giardia.
Symptomatic for 4 weeks with malabsorption; treat it.
For C. difficile.
